content: The High Rising Terminal (HRT), also referred to as uptalk, upspeak, or High Rising Intonation (HRI), is a linguistic feature observed in certain English accents. It is characterized by a rising intonation pattern on the final syllable or syllables of a statement. According to Ladd (1996), in American and Australian English, HRT is marked by a high tone (a high pitch or fundamental frequency) that begins on the final accented syllable near the end of the statement and continues to rise in frequency, sometimes by as much as 40%, until the end of the intonational phrase. Recent research, such as that by Warren (2005), indicates that the rise in pitch can occur on one or more syllables following the last accented syllable of the phrase, and the range of this rise is more variable than previously understood. Origins The origins of HRT remain uncertain. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the American English variety may have originated on the West Coast, ranging from Southern California to the Pacific Northwest. In the Southern Hemisphere, Allan (1990) proposed that HRT may have originated in New Zealand. It is unclear whether the American and Oceanic varieties influenced each other in the spread of this feature. Usage In the United States, HRT is a relatively recent phenomenon but is becoming increasingly common, particularly among younger speakers. Ching (1982) provides one of the earliest accounts of HRT in American English. However, linguistic research on HRT has a longer history in journals from Australia, New Zealand, and Britain, where it was noted as early as World War II. In Sydney, younger generations use HRT more than twice as often as older generations, with women being the primary users (Guy et al., 1986). HRT can serve conversational functions, such as encouraging the listener to participate in the conversation, and these functions are more frequently employed by women. Additionally, it subtly signals that the speaker has not finished speaking, potentially discouraging interruptions (Allen, 1990; Guy et al., 1986; Warren, 2005). HRT has also been observed in speech patterns in Canada, Cape Town, the Falkland Islands, and the United States. In the U.S., it is often associated with a specific sociolect that originated among affluent teenage girls in Southern California, commonly referred to as Valspeak or the Valley girl accent. In rural parts of North Dakota and Minnesota, HRT is characteristic of speech influenced by the Norwegian language due to migration patterns. In Britain, HRT is sometimes ridiculed as Australian Questioning Intonation and is attributed to the popularity of Australian soap operas among teenagers. However, HRT is also a feature of several regional UK dialects, including those of Bristol, East Anglia, and Northern Ireland. It is frequently heard in some Irish accents and is a significant component of the DORT accent, a satirical term for the pronunciation of the DART train line in Dublin's affluent suburbs, where this accent is most prevalent. This trend, along with others in middle-class Ireland, has been humorously critiqued in the fictional Ross O'Carroll-Kelly diaries by journalist Paul Howard. Misconceptions HRT is often mistakenly referred to as questioning intonation, but this term is not widely used by linguists because not all questions exhibit rising intonation. In fact, most sentences using a Wh-interrogative rise and then fall at the end. While HRT has been negatively portrayed in popular media in Australia, Britain, and the United States as a sign of insecurity in the speaker, more recent evidence (McLemore, 1991; Cheng et al., 2005; Warren, 2005) suggests that assertive speakers and leaders within peer groups are more likely to use HRT in their declarative statements than junior members of the group. For example, University of Pennsylvania phonologist Mark Liberman has noted that George W. Bush began using HRT extensively in his later speeches. References in Popular Culture In the Family Guy episode Whistle While Your Wife Works, Stewie mocks Brian's girlfriend for speaking with HRT, describing it as where everything has a question mark at the end of it, with an upward inflection. Additionally, Stephen Fry humorously condemned this speech pattern to Room 101 in the BBC TV series, referring to it as Australian Question Intonation (AQI).
